1

Read the Design

These are design questions first, query questions second.

  1. A3.2.2 ERD

    Identify the junction table and explain why it represents a many-to-many relationship.

  2. A3.2.4 Composite key

    State the composite primary key in MEMBERSHIP and explain why both columns are needed together.

  3. A3.2.2 One-to-one

    Explain why LOGIN_ACCOUNT to STUDENT is one-to-one in this dataset.

  4. A3.2.3 Data types

    Explain why YearGroup is stored as an integer, while Username and MeetingRoom are text fields. Give one possible problem caused by choosing the wrong type.

2

Filtering and Distinct Values

Query one table at a time before you join them together.

Syntax reference — WHERE, DISTINCT, LIKE 
-- Filter by a value
SELECT * FROM CLUB WHERE MeetingDay = 'Thursday';

-- Unique values, sorted
SELECT DISTINCT Role FROM MEMBERSHIP ORDER BY Role;

-- LIKE pattern matching — % is the wildcard
SELECT * FROM CLUB WHERE MeetingRoom LIKE '%Lab%';

-- Exact text match (case-sensitive in most engines)
SELECT * FROM STUDENT WHERE LastName = 'Khan';

DISTINCT applies to the entire row of selected columns, not just the first one. Combine with ORDER BY for tidy output.

  1. A3.3.2 WHERE

    List every club that meets on Thursday.

  2. A3.3.2 DISTINCT

    Return each unique role used in the MEMBERSHIP table, sorted alphabetically.

  3. A3.3.2 LIKE

    Find clubs where the meeting room contains the word Lab.

  4. A3.3.2 WHERE

    Show the first names, last names, and year groups of both students whose surname is Khan.

3

Join Through Relationships

Move from entity table to entity table using foreign keys.

Syntax reference — JOIN through a junction table 
-- Two-table join (one-to-one)
SELECT s.FirstName, s.LastName, a.Username, a.LastLoginDate
FROM STUDENT s
INNER JOIN LOGIN_ACCOUNT a ON s.StudentID = a.StudentID;

-- Three-table join via junction table (many-to-many)
-- STUDENT ↔ MEMBERSHIP ↔ CLUB
SELECT s.FirstName, s.LastName, m.Role, c.ClubName
FROM STUDENT s
INNER JOIN MEMBERSHIP m ON s.StudentID = m.StudentID
INNER JOIN CLUB c       ON m.ClubID    = c.ClubID
WHERE c.ClubName = 'Coding Collective'
ORDER BY m.Role, s.LastName;

With a junction table you always join twice: first to the junction, then from the junction to the other entity. Every row in MEMBERSHIP connects one student to one club.

  1. A3.3.2 JOIN 2 tables

    Join STUDENT to LOGIN_ACCOUNT and show each student's full name, username, and last login date.

  2. A3.3.2 JOIN 3 tables

    Show every member of Coding Collective with their role and year group. Sort by role, then last name.

  3. A3.3.2 JOIN 3 tables

    List the club name, meeting day, student full name, and role for all memberships. Order first by meeting day, then club name.

  4. A3.3.2 Filter joined data

    Show only Year 12 students and the clubs they attend.

  5. A3.3.2 Date filter

    Return usernames and last-login dates for accounts that were used on or after 2026-03-09.

Schema and ERD Thinking

Use the dataset to explain the database design, not just query it.

  1. A3.2.1 Schema levels

    Give one example of what belongs in the conceptual schema, logical schema, and physical schema for this clubs system.

  2. A3.2.2 Modality

    Explain the likely modality between STUDENT and LOGIN_ACCOUNT, then compare it with the modality between STUDENT and MEMBERSHIP.

5

DDL and DML Practice

Make structural and row-level changes after you finish the earlier sections.

Syntax reference — CREATE TABLE with FK, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE 
-- Create a table that references CLUB
CREATE TABLE EVENT (
    EventID   INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
    ClubID    INTEGER,
    EventName TEXT,
    EventDate DATE,
    FOREIGN KEY (ClubID) REFERENCES CLUB(ClubID)
);

-- Insert a row
INSERT INTO EVENT (EventID, ClubID, EventName, EventDate)
VALUES (1, 101, 'Hack Night', '2026-04-15');

-- Update a row — always use WHERE
UPDATE MEMBERSHIP
SET Role = 'Coordinator'
WHERE StudentID = 5 AND ClubID = 101;

-- Delete a specific row
DELETE FROM EVENT WHERE EventID = 1;

When updating a row in a composite-key table (like MEMBERSHIP) you must include all parts of the key in the WHERE clause to identify exactly one row.

  1. A3.3.1 CREATE TABLE

    Create a table called EVENT with EventID as the primary key, plus ClubID, EventName, and EventDate. Link ClubID back to CLUB.

  2. A3.3.3 INSERT

    Insert a new event called Hack Night for Coding Collective on a date of your choice.

  3. A3.3.3 UPDATE

    Update Omar James's role in Coding Collective from Member to Coordinator.

  4. A3.3.3 DELETE

    Delete the Hack Night event you inserted.

After DDL and DML work, reload Campus Clubs in the playground to restore the original sample dataset.

Model Answers — Campus Clubs

Section 1 — Read the Design

1
Junction table MEMBERSHIP is the junction table. It has a row for each student–club pairing, so one student can join many clubs and one club can have many students — a many-to-many relationship.
2
Composite key The composite primary key is (StudentID, ClubID). Neither column alone is unique — a student can join multiple clubs (same StudentID, different ClubID) and a club has multiple members (same ClubID, different StudentID). Together they uniquely identify one membership.
3
One-to-one Each student has exactly one login account and each login account belongs to exactly one student. The foreign key in LOGIN_ACCOUNT is also a unique key, preventing more than one account per student.
4
Data types YearGroup is an integer because arithmetic comparisons (e.g. YearGroup = 12) are needed and it never contains letters. Storing it as text would cause incorrect sort order (11 sorts before 9 alphabetically). If MeetingRoom were an integer, values like "Lab B" could not be stored.

Section 2 — Filtering and Distinct Values

1 
SELECT * FROM CLUB WHERE MeetingDay = 'Thursday';
2 
SELECT DISTINCT Role FROM MEMBERSHIP ORDER BY Role;
3 
SELECT * FROM CLUB WHERE MeetingRoom LIKE '%Lab%';
4 
SELECT FirstName, LastName, YearGroup
FROM STUDENT
WHERE LastName = 'Khan';

Section 3 — Join Through Relationships

1 
SELECT s.FirstName, s.LastName, a.Username, a.LastLoginDate
FROM STUDENT s
INNER JOIN LOGIN_ACCOUNT a ON s.StudentID = a.StudentID;
2 
SELECT s.FirstName, s.LastName, m.Role, s.YearGroup
FROM STUDENT s
INNER JOIN MEMBERSHIP m ON s.StudentID = m.StudentID
INNER JOIN CLUB c       ON m.ClubID    = c.ClubID
WHERE c.ClubName = 'Coding Collective'
ORDER BY m.Role, s.LastName;
3 
SELECT c.ClubName, c.MeetingDay,
       s.FirstName, s.LastName, m.Role
FROM STUDENT s
INNER JOIN MEMBERSHIP m ON s.StudentID = m.StudentID
INNER JOIN CLUB c       ON m.ClubID    = c.ClubID
ORDER BY c.MeetingDay, c.ClubName;
4 
SELECT s.FirstName, s.LastName, c.ClubName
FROM STUDENT s
INNER JOIN MEMBERSHIP m ON s.StudentID = m.StudentID
INNER JOIN CLUB c       ON m.ClubID    = c.ClubID
WHERE s.YearGroup = 12;
5 
SELECT a.Username, a.LastLoginDate
FROM LOGIN_ACCOUNT a
WHERE a.LastLoginDate >= '2026-03-09';

Section 4 — Schema and ERD Thinking

1
Schema levels Conceptual: "Student joins Club" entity relationship. Logical: STUDENT table with StudentID INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, ClubName VARCHAR(100), composite key (StudentID, ClubID) in MEMBERSHIP. Physical: B-tree index on StudentID for fast membership lookups.
2
Modality STUDENT to LOGIN_ACCOUNT: mandatory on both sides — every student must have exactly one account. STUDENT to MEMBERSHIP: optional — a student may exist without joining any club (zero memberships is valid).
3
Referential integrity The MEMBERSHIP table has a foreign key on ClubID referencing CLUB(ClubID). If ClubID does not exist in CLUB, the database rejects the insert — preventing a membership record that points to a non-existent club.

Section 5 — DDL and DML Practice

1 
CREATE TABLE EVENT (
    EventID   INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
    ClubID    INTEGER,
    EventName TEXT,
    EventDate DATE,
    FOREIGN KEY (ClubID) REFERENCES CLUB(ClubID)
);
2 
-- Coding Collective ClubID must match actual data; assume 101
INSERT INTO EVENT (EventID, ClubID, EventName, EventDate)
VALUES (1, 101, 'Hack Night', '2026-04-15');
3 
-- Find Omar James's StudentID first, then:
UPDATE MEMBERSHIP
SET Role = 'Coordinator'
WHERE StudentID = (SELECT StudentID FROM STUDENT
                   WHERE FirstName = 'Omar' AND LastName = 'James')
  AND ClubID   = (SELECT ClubID FROM CLUB WHERE ClubName = 'Coding Collective');
4 
DELETE FROM EVENT WHERE EventName = 'Hack Night';
